units.title: Comparatives and superlatives (with less and as ... as)
notes: Short adjectives: -er than, the -est: This bridge is longer than that one. It is the longest bridge in the country.
Long adjectives: more and the most: The subway is more crowded than the ferry.
less + adjective is the opposite of more: The countryside is less noisy than the city.
as + adjective + as when two things are the same: The tower is as tall as the castle. Irregular: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; far, further, furthest.

items.q: The motorway is ___ than the old road through the tunnel.
This is ___ skyscraper in the city. You can see it from everywhere.
My neighbourhood is ___ crowded than the city centre. It's very quiet.
The ferry isn't as fast ___ the train.
The traffic today is ___ than yesterday. We haven't moved for an hour!
The stadium is the ___ building in our town.
A taxi is ___ expensive than the subway.
The island is ___ from the city than the castle.
The cable car is the ___ way to get to the top of the mountain.
items.why: easy: y changes to i, then -est

items.q: The fountain in the main square is ___ (pretty) than the one in the park.
items.why: pretty: y changes to i, then -er

items.q: Tokyo is one of the ___ (busy) cities in the world.
For pedestrians, the old town is ___ (safe) than the motorway.
The new exhibit is the ___ (interesting) one in the whole museum.
I think the view from the tower is ___ (good) than the view from the bridge.
The field is as ___ (big) as the stadium. They are the same size.
items.why: between as and as the adjective doesn't change

items.q: The castle is more old than the bridge.
a: The castle is older than the bridge.

items.q: It is the most beautiful fountain of the city.
a: It is the most beautiful fountain in the city.
items.why: after a superlative we say in the city

items.q: The train is as quick than the taxi.
a: The train is as quick as the taxi.

items.q: the steeple / is / point / the highest / in / the village
a: The steeple is the highest point in the village.
The highest point in the village is the steeple.

items.q: less / than / it / noisy / is / the city centre / much
a: It is much less noisy than the city centre.

units.title: Modal verbs: must, mustn't, should, might, could, would
notes: Modal + base verb, with no to and no -s: You must rest. She might have the flu.
must for obligation, mustn't for prohibition, don't have to when it is not necessary: You mustn't run here. You don't have to pay.
should and shouldn't for advice: You should put a bandage on your ankle.
might and could for possibility; Could you and Would you for polite requests and offers: It might be an infection. Could you help me?

items.q: You've got a sore throat. You ___ drink something warm.
You ___ touch that rash. It will get worse.
I'm not sure, but it ___ be chickenpox. Let's ask the doctor.
___ you pass me the bandage, please?
It's Saturday tomorrow, so we ___ get up early.
He might ___ the flu. He has a headache and a runny nose.
You ___ wash your hands before you touch the cut. It's very important.
Her ankle hurts a lot. She ___ play football today.
items.why: it is a bad idea: shouldn't

items.q: ___ you like me to call the doctor?
This medicine is only for adults. Children ___ (must) take it.
You have indigestion again. You ___ (should) eat so fast.
items.why: eating fast is a bad idea: shouldn't

items.q: She should ___ (put) some ice on her wrist.
Could you ___ (open) the window, please? I've got a headache.
The nurse has lots of bandages, so you ___ (not have to) bring one.
items.why: it isn't necessary: don't have to

items.q: My brother sprained his ankle, so he ___ (must) rest for a week. The doctor said so.
items.why: the doctor's order is an obligation

items.q: You should to see a doctor.
You don't must run in the hospital.
a: You mustn't run in the hospital.
You must not run in the hospital.
items.why: the negative of must is mustn't

items.q: It might rains later.
a bandage / on / should / your elbow / you / put
a: You should put a bandage on your elbow.

items.q: tell / could / where / me / you / is / the hospital
a: Could you tell me where the hospital is?
items.why: after tell me where, the verb goes last

units.title: Subject and object pronouns; Reported speech
notes: Subject pronouns go before the verb: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Object pronouns go after a verb or a preposition: me, you, him, her, it, us, them. She helps me. Look at them.
Reported speech: the present simple changes to the past simple and the present continuous to the past continuous: 'I need a password,' he said. He said he needed a password.
Pronouns change too: 'My inbox is full,' said Eva. Eva said her inbox was full.
Reported orders: told + person + to or not to + verb: She told us to log in.

items.q: I can't find my password. Can you help ___?
items.why: object pronoun after the verb help

items.q: These files are important. Don't delete ___.
My brother and I love this game. Dad downloaded it for ___.
Laura forgot her device, so I lent ___ my tablet.
Mr Evans is our ICT teacher. ___ teaches us to use the cloud safely.
'I am uploading the photos,' said Tom. Tom said he ___ the photos.
items.why: am uploading changes to was uploading

items.q: 'We need a new browser,' said the girls. The girls said ___ needed a new browser.
'Don't share your password,' the teacher told us. The teacher told us ___ our password.
'My laptop is broken,' said Ana. Ana said ___ laptop was broken.
This bookmark is for Dan. Please give it to ___ (he).
items.why: after to use the object pronoun him

items.q: My friends are online. I'm chatting with ___ (they) now.
items.why: after with use the object pronoun them

items.q: 'I use the same password for everything,' said Leo. Leo said he ___ (use) the same password for everything.
'Click on the home page,' she told me. She told me ___ (click) on the home page.
'The printer doesn't have any ink,' said Dad. Dad said the printer ___ (not have) any ink.
items.why: doesn't have changes to didn't have

items.q: 'We are changing our privacy settings,' they said. They said they ___ (change) their privacy settings.
items.why: are changing changes to were changing

items.q: The teacher sent we an email.
a: The teacher sent us an email.
items.why: after a verb use the object pronoun us

items.q: He said me that the file was in the cloud.
a: He told me that the file was in the cloud.
He said that the file was in the cloud.
He said to me that the file was in the cloud.
items.why: told + person, or said without a person

items.q: Dad told me log out of his computer.
a: Dad told me to log out of his computer.

items.q: told / the teacher / our names / us / in / to write / lowercase letters
a: The teacher told us to write our names in lowercase letters.

items.q: said / was / her inbox / she / full / that
a: She said that her inbox was full.

units.title: Past simple: affirmative, negative and questions
notes: Regular verbs add -ed: pack, packed; decide, decided; plan, planned. Irregular verbs change: go, went; choose, chose; read, read.
Negative: didn't + base verb: We didn't reserve a room.
Questions: Did + subject + base verb: Did you pack your suitcase? Yes, I did.
Use it for finished actions in the past, with yesterday, last year, two days ago.

items.q: Last summer we ___ at a campsite near the beach.
Last month they ___ a guidebook for their trip to Rome.
We didn't ___ our luggage at the airport.
items.why: after didn't use the base verb

items.q: ___ you read the brochure about the hotel yesterday?
Did she pack her rucksack last night? No, she ___.
Where ___ you go on holiday last year?
items.why: question word + did + subject + base verb

items.q: My grandad ___ suspicious when he saw the open suitcase.
Two weeks ago we ___ our destination with a map and a coin.
I ___ the itinerary because it was too long.
My aunt ___ (plan) the whole trip two months ago.
We ___ (not reserve) a room, so we slept in the car that night.
Yesterday I ___ (read) the whole guidebook in one afternoon.
items.why: read is irregular: the past is read

items.q: ___ (do) your parents choose the accommodation last year?
Dad ___ (carry) all the suitcases to the hotel yesterday.
items.why: carry: y changes to i, then -ed

items.q: We ___ (see) all the famous sights when we were in London last spring.
Did you visited the castle last weekend?
a: Did you visit the castle last weekend?
items.why: after Did use the base verb

items.q: We didn't went to the campsite.
a: We didn't go to the campsite.
We did not go to the campsite.
items.why: after didn't use the base verb

items.q: Yesterday I have packed my rucksack.
did / for / pay / the accommodation / how much / you
a: How much did you pay for the accommodation?
items.why: question word + did + subject + base verb

items.q: didn't / our / to the campsite / bring / we / heavy luggage
a: We didn't bring our heavy luggage to the campsite.

units.title: Present continuous; Active and passive voice
notes: Present continuous: am, is or are + verb-ing for actions happening now: The plane is taking off.
We also use it for fixed future plans: We are flying to Rome next Friday.
Passive: be + past participle. Present: Passports are checked at security. Past: The telephone was invented in 1876.
Use by for the person who does the action: The plane was flown by a young pilot.

items.q: Look! The passengers ___ the plane now.
We ___ to Dublin next Saturday. We've already got the tickets.
What ___ the flight attendant carrying?
items.why: the flight attendant is he or she: is

items.q: She ___ at the gate. She's still in the check-in area.
All carry-on bags ___ at security every day.
items.why: bags don't check, people check them: passive

items.q: The first aeroplane ___ by the Wright brothers in 1903.
Our flight was delayed ___ a storm.
Hand luggage ___ in the space above the seats.
items.why: luggage is singular: is + past participle

items.q: The radio ___ invented in the nineteenth century.
Be quiet, please. The pilot ___ (speak) to the passengers right now.
My cousins ___ (arrive) on a connecting flight tomorrow morning. Their tickets are booked.
I ___ (not use) my camera at the moment. You can borrow it.
items.why: at the moment: am not + verb-ing

items.q: Boarding passes ___ (show) at the gate before every flight.
The bicycle ___ (invent) more than two hundred years ago.
These wheels ___ (make) in Germany last year.
The plane is take off now.
a: The plane is taking off now.

items.q: The passports was checked by a police officer.
a: The passports were checked by a police officer.

items.q: The telephone was invented for Alexander Graham Bell.
a: The telephone was invented by Alexander Graham Bell.

items.q: is / to / my family / next month / Canada / flying
a: My family is flying to Canada next month.
Next month my family is flying to Canada.

items.q: was / by / the flight attendant / served / lunch
a: Lunch was served by the flight attendant.

units.title: Present perfect with for and since; Past simple with ago
notes: Present perfect: have or has + past participle for something that started in the past and continues now: We have had this dishwasher for two years.
for + a period of time: for three days, for a long time. since + the starting point: since Monday, since 2020, since I was five.
ago goes with the past simple for finished actions: I made my bed ten minutes ago.
Ask with How long: How long have you lived here?

items.q: The washing machine has been broken ___ last Tuesday.
items.why: last Tuesday is a starting point: since

items.q: I have done the ironing in this house ___ two years.
items.why: two years is a period: for

items.q: Dad swept the attic three days ___.
My sister ___ the dishes every evening since she was eight.
How long ___ you had that old vacuum cleaner?
We ___ the vacuum cleaner two years ago.
Grandma has ___ breakfast for the family for forty years.
items.why: make breakfast; has + past participle made

items.q: He ___ his bed since Monday!
I ___ this mop for five years and it still works.
items.why: from the past until now: present perfect

items.q: My mum ___ (work) from home since 2020, and she loves it.
I ___ (know) my best friend for six years.
items.why: for six years until now: have known

items.q: We ___ (clean) the whole attic two weeks ago.
The lock on the door ___ (be) broken since Christmas. We need a new one.
items.why: since Christmas until now: has been

items.q: Tom hates chores. He ___ (not do) the laundry for a month!
items.why: for a month until now: hasn't done

items.q: I ___ (hang) the washing outside an hour ago, and now it is raining!
items.why: ago needs the past simple; hang, hung

items.q: I live in this house since 2019.
a: I have lived in this house since 2019.
I've lived in this house since 2019.

items.q: We have had this dishwasher since three years.
a: We have had this dishwasher for three years.
items.why: three years is a period: for

items.q: She has ironed her shirt ten minutes ago.
a: She ironed her shirt ten minutes ago.

items.q: have / how long / you / that broom / had
a: How long have you had that broom?
items.why: How long + have + subject + past participle

items.q: hasn't / for / my brother / a week / his room / vacuumed
a: My brother hasn't vacuumed his room for a week.
items.why: for + period goes at the end

units.title: Past perfect; Quantifiers (some, any, a lot of, a few, a little)
notes: Past perfect: had + past participle for the action that happened first: When we arrived, the parade had already started.
Negative: hadn't + past participle. Question: Had you seen fireworks before?
Countable nouns: a few, many, How many: a few lanterns. Uncountable nouns: a little, much, How much: a little gunpowder.
some in affirmative sentences, any in negatives and questions, a lot of with both kinds of noun: There aren't any pumpkins.

items.q: When we got to the square, the parade ___ already finished.
items.why: it finished before we got there: had

items.q: I had never ___ a real bonfire before that night.
She didn't go to the party because she ___ made a costume.
By the time the fireworks started, the children ___ asleep.
___ you ever visited Scotland before last summer?
items.why: before a past time: Had + participle

items.q: There were only ___ lanterns left in the shop, so we bought three.
We haven't got ___ pumpkins for Halloween.
How ___ gunpowder do they use in the fireworks?
There were ___ people at the parade. The streets were full!
items.why: people is countable and plural: a lot of

items.q: By the time we found our seats, the parade ___ (start).
items.why: by the time + earlier action: had started

items.q: When Mum looked for the witch costume, my sister ___ (already take) it.
items.why: already goes between had and the participle

items.q: Paula was nervous on the plane to Mexico. She ___ (never fly) before.
items.why: before that past moment: had never flown

items.q: When I opened my bag, I saw that I ___ (leave) my lantern at home.
items.why: leaving it happened first: had left

items.q: The show was sold out, and we ___ (not buy) our tickets yet, so we went home.
When we arrived, the dragon dance ___ (already begin), so we missed the start.
items.why: begin, began, begun: had already begun

items.q: When I arrived, the parade has already started.
a: When I arrived, the parade had already started.
items.why: earlier past action: had, not has

items.q: There were much people at the festival.
a: There were a lot of people at the festival.
There were many people at the festival.
There were lots of people at the festival.
items.why: people is countable: many or a lot of

items.q: We didn't see some fireworks.
had / the fireworks / when / we / finished / arrived
a: The fireworks had finished when we arrived.
When we arrived, the fireworks had finished.

items.q: a few / in / there / ghosts / were / the parade / only
a: There were only a few ghosts in the parade.
In the parade there were only a few ghosts.

units.title: First conditional
notes: If + present simple, will or won't + base verb: If the river rises, the town will flood.
Use it for real possibilities in the future.
Don't use will in the if part: If it doesn't rain (not if it won't rain), there will be a drought.
The if part can come second, without a comma: We will stay at home if there is a blizzard.

items.q: If it doesn't rain soon, there ___ a drought this summer.
If the volcano ___ tomorrow, people will leave the island.
We ___ to the lake on Sunday if there is a thunderstorm.
If people ___ careful with barbecues this summer, there will be forest fires.
items.why: after if: present simple of be

items.q: What ___ you do if the river floods your street next week?
items.why: floods is present, so the result takes will

items.q: If the blizzard ___ tonight, the school will be closed tomorrow.
If we plant more trees, the desert ___ grow so fast.
items.why: will not is won't, then base verb

items.q: You will see the waterfall if you ___ north along the river tomorrow.
___ the animals escape if there is a fire in the jungle?
items.why: question about a future result: Will

items.q: If the hurricane ___ (arrive) tomorrow, we will stay in the basement.
items.why: after if: present simple, it arrives

items.q: The beach ___ (disappear) one day if the sea keeps rising.
If we ___ (not save) water this summer, the lake will dry up.
Don't worry. If there is an earthquake during our trip next week, the guide ___ (tell) us what to do.
We ___ (not climb) the mountain tomorrow if the weather is bad.
If she ___ (travel) east next summer, she will see the desert.
items.why: after if: present simple, she travels

items.q: If it will snow tonight, we will make a snowman.
a: If it snows tonight, we will make a snowman.
If it snows tonight, we'll make a snowman.

items.q: If the river floods, we will to move to my aunt's house.
a: If the river floods, we will move to my aunt's house.
If the river floods, we'll move to my aunt's house.

items.q: If the storm gets worse, we stay at home tomorrow.
a: If the storm gets worse, we will stay at home tomorrow.
If the storm gets worse, we'll stay at home tomorrow.

items.q: rains / if / will / too much / the fields / it / flood
a: If it rains too much, the fields will flood.
The fields will flood if it rains too much.

items.q: we / if / you / turn up late / won't / wait for you
a: We won't wait for you if you turn up late.
If you turn up late, we won't wait for you.

units.title: Second conditional; Conditionals review
notes: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb, for imaginary situations: If I had wings, I would fly.
With be we often use were for all persons: If I were you, I'd train harder.
First conditional for real future possibilities: If it rains, we'll stay in. Zero conditional for facts: If you heat water, it boils.
Short forms: I'd, you'd, wouldn't.

items.q: If I ___ a rock star, I would travel around the world.
If she trained every day, she ___ the marathon.
items.why: if + past, so would + base verb

items.q: What ___ you do if you saw a lion on safari?
If I ___ enough money, I would try bungee jumping.
items.why: no would after if: past simple

items.q: He ___ go rafting if he couldn't swim.
If you ___ water to 100 degrees, it boils.
items.why: a fact: present simple in both parts

items.q: If it's sunny tomorrow, we ___ water skiing.
items.why: real possibility: first conditional with will

items.q: If we ___ near the sea, we would go windsurfing every day.
items.why: would in the result, past simple after if

items.q: If I were you, I ___ the sequel. It's brilliant.
items.why: advice: If I were you, I would

items.q: If I ___ (meet) a famous athlete, I would ask for a photo.
items.why: would in the result, so past simple: met

items.q: If we had a boat, we ___ (go) diving every weekend.
My sister is scared of heights. She ___ (not try) paragliding if you paid her!
items.why: paid is past, so wouldn't try

items.q: If Marta ___ (not be) so shy, she would join the gymnastics team.
items.why: imaginary: past of be after if

items.q: Look at those clouds. If it ___ (rain) this afternoon, we will play table tennis inside.
items.why: will in the result: present simple after if

items.q: When you ___ (drop) a bowling ball, it falls fast.
items.why: a fact: present simple in both parts

items.q: If I would have a horse, I would ride it every day.
a: If I had a horse, I would ride it every day.
If I had a horse, I'd ride it every day.
items.why: no would after if: use the past simple

items.q: If he practised more, he will be a champion.
a: If he practised more, he would be a champion.
If he practises more, he will be a champion.
items.why: past goes with would, present goes with will

items.q: If I were you, I don't go skating on that lake.
a: If I were you, I wouldn't go skating on that lake.
If I were you, I would not go skating on that lake.
items.why: If I were you, I wouldn't + base verb

items.q: a globetrotter / I / if / would / every country / were / visit / I
a: If I were a globetrotter, I would visit every country.
I would visit every country if I were a globetrotter.

items.q: you / what / would / do / won / if / you / a gold medal
a: What would you do if you won a gold medal?
If you won a gold medal, what would you do?
